an up-to-date inventory is kept of every training-data source, including its origin, responsible party, license, collection method, intended use constraints, and processing history.
data integrity is provided when training data is stored and transferred.
integrity monitoring is applied to guard against unauthorized modifications or corruption of training data.
datasets are watermarked so their use can be attributed and any unauthorized use detected.
labeling platforms enforce access controls that restrict who can create, modify, or approve annotations.
cryptographic integrity is applied to labeling artifacts.
sensitive information in labels is redacted, anonymized, or encrypted before being used in any labeling artifact.
training and fine-tuning pipelines implement poisoning detection techniques to identify potential data poisoning or unintentional corruption in training data.

requirements.text: input normalization is applied before tokenization or embedding.
encoding and representation smuggling in inputs is detected and mitigated. Approved mitigations include canonicalization, strict schema validation, policy-based rejection, or explicit marking.
all inputs that could steer model behavior are treated as untrusted and screened by a prompt injection detection ruleset or classifier, with flagged inputs blocked.
input length controls prevent content from exceeding the context window. The controls must reject inputs that exceed token limits rather than truncating them.

the system implements a character set restriction for all inputs. The restriction must use an allow-list approach derived from the languages and use cases the system supports, permitting only characters that are explicitly required.

the system enforces an instruction hierarchy in which system and developer messages override user instructions and other untrusted inputs, even after user instructions have been processed. Untrusted content cannot acquire higher instruction priority through retrieval, tool processing, or persistence across conversation turns.
reserved special tokens are encoded as literal characters and cannot be injected into the model context.
the system can detect many-shot jailbreaking patterns.

every prompt is scored by a content classifier for violence, self-harm, hate, and sexual content against configurable thresholds. Prompts that exceed those thresholds are rejected or sanitized before reaching the model context.
prompt content classification is evaluated for unsupported languages.
non-text inputs (image/video/audio) are checked for adversarial perturbations, steganographic payloads, hidden or embedded content, or known attack patterns.
coordinated attacks spanning multiple input types (e.g., steganographic payloads in images combined with prompt injection in text) are detected and blocked.
a model registry maintains an inventory of all deployed model artifacts and their origin.
all model artifacts (weights, configurations, tokenizers, base models, fine-tunes, adapters, and safety/policy models) are cryptographically signed by authorized entities.
model cryptographic signatures are verified at deployment admission and on load.
models undergo automated input validation testing, safety evaluation testing, and output sanitization testing before deployment.
models subjected to post-training quantization are re-evaluated against the same safety and alignment test suite on the compressed artifact before deployment.
provider model, version, or routing changes trigger security re-evaluation before continued use.
production deployments implement rollout mechanisms with automated rollback triggers.
rollback capabilities restore the complete model state.
model versions running in parallel use isolated runtime state so that AI-specific shared resources are not shared across deployments.
AI-specific runtime components are not shared across environment boundaries (e.g., development, staging, production).
model training and fine-tuning environments are isolated from production environments.
models used in RLHF fine-tuning are versioned and integrity-verified before use in a training run.
RLHF training stages include automated detection of reward hacking or reward model over-optimization.
in multi-stage fine-tuning pipelines, each stage's output is integrity-verified before it is consumed by the next stage.
fine-tuning checkpoints are registered as distinct artifacts.
AI models execute in isolated sandboxes.
model artifact loading enforces an explicit allow-list of serialization formats that do not permit arbitrary code execution during deserialization.
workload attestation is performed before model loading to provide proof that the execution environment has not been tampered with.
confidential inference services protect model weights during runtime through isolated execution environments.
AI accelerator (GPU) firmware is version-pinned, signed, and attested at boot.
execution within a trusted execution environment (TEE) provides hardware-enforced isolation, memory encryption, and integrity protection.
AI accelerator (GPU) integrity is validated using hardware-based attestation mechanisms before each workload executes.
accelerator (GPU) memory is isolated between workloads through partitioning mechanisms with memory sanitization between jobs.
accelerator interconnects are restricted to approved topologies and authenticated endpoints.
edge AI devices authenticate to central infrastructure using strong authentication mechanisms.
models deployed to edge or mobile devices are cryptographically signed during packaging, and that the on-device runtime validates these signatures or checksums before loading or inference.
inference runtimes enforce process, memory, and file access isolation.
model weights and sensitive parameters stored locally are encrypted using hardware-backed key stores or secure enclaves.

models packaged within mobile, IoT, or embedded applications are encrypted at rest, and decrypted only inside a trusted runtime or secure enclave, preventing direct extraction from the app package or filesystem.
high-risk AI operations (model deployment, weight export, training data access, production configuration changes) require step-up authentication.

vectors that fall outside normal clustering patterns are flagged and quarantined before entering production indices.
no component reachable from agent execution can write agent outputs or tool outputs to trusted agent memory without explicit source validation.
content crafted to manipulate retrieval results is detected and rejected or quarantined before vectorization.
new content written to memory is checked for contradictions with what is already stored and that conflicts trigger alerts.
expired vectors are excluded from retrieval results.
memory can be reset.
quarantined content is retained but excluded from all retrieval results.
per-tool quotas and timeouts (e.g., CPU, memory, disk, egress, and execution time) are enforced by the runtime.

requirements.section_title: High-Impact Action Approval and Irreversibility Controls

requirements.text: the AI-augmented review mechanism is protected against manipulation by adversarial inputs, and cannot be overridden or bypassed through prompt injection.

requirements.text: each tool/plugin executes in a least-privilege sandbox or is otherwise isolated from model operations.
tool outputs are validated against schemas.

the runtime enforces the privileges, resource limits, and output-validation requirements declared in tool manifests.
components processing untrusted data are isolated from tool-calling capabilities, ensuring that compromised data processing cannot trigger unauthorized tool invocations.
there is architectural separation between processing of untrusted tool outputs and agent operations.
external resources named in model output are verified against an approved allow-list or registry before the agent installs or invokes them.
policy violations trigger automatic containment of affected tools, such as stopping their execution, isolating them, or revoking their permissions.
services reachable from agent or tool sandboxes enforce the defined run, task, or tenant isolation policy on agent-writable state, including object names.
each agent instance has a unique cryptographic identity and authenticates as a first-class principal to downstream systems.
agent-initiated actions are cryptographically bound to each step of the execution chain for non-repudiation.
agent identity credentials rotate on a defined schedule.
agent state persisted between invocations is integrity-protected.
agent actions are authorized against fine-grained policies enforced by the runtime that restrict which tools an agent may invoke, and which parameter values it may supply.

when a human-approval gate is not satisfied within the defined approval time, the system blocks the pending action.
kill-switch commands are implemented through an out-of-band channel that is isolated from the agent runtime.
MCP components are obtained only from trusted sources and cryptographically verified.
only allow-listed MCP servers are permitted.
locally launched MCP servers run in a least-privilege sandbox with restricted file system, network, and system access.
MCP servers validate access tokens for each request and do not rely on transport security alone.
MCP servers validate the presented access token's issuer, audience, expiration, and scope claims in accordance with OAuth 2.1.
MCP servers acting as OAuth 2.1 resource servers do not store or persist access tokens or user credentials.
MCP tools/list returns only tools permitted by the requester's authorized scopes, and that list responses vary only by authorization context, never by connection.
MCP servers enforce access control on every tool invocation, validating that the user's access token authorizes both the requested tool and the specific argument values supplied.
Requirement removed.
MCP servers only accept tokens explicitly issued for them, and do not pass tokens issued for other services through to downstream APIs.
MCP servers protect the integrity of `requestState` that influences authorization, resource access, or business logic, and reject state that fails verification.
MCP clients bind persisted OAuth client credentials to the issuing authorization server and do not present them to a different authorization server.
MCP servers enforce single use server-side for `requestState` that must be consumed at most once.
authenticated, encrypted streamable HTTP is used for MCP transport for remote services.
stdio transport is permitted only in controlled local environments.
MCP servers validate both the Origin header and the Host header independently on all HTTP-based transports to prevent DNS rebinding attacks.
MCP clients enforce a minimum acceptable protocol version and do not retry with, or fall back to, a protocol version or legacy handshake below that minimum.
access tokens between the MCP client and server are sender-constrained using mTLS or DPoP.
MCP intermediaries enforcing policy on mirrored request headers confirm that the protocol version indicates a revision requiring header and body validation before trusting those headers.
MCP tools/list and tools/call responses are validated against their declared schemas before being injected into the model context.
MCP tools/list and tools/call responses are screened for indirect prompt injection before being injected into the model context.
MCP servers reject unrecognized or oversized parameters in function calls.
all MCP servers enforce strict schema validation.
all MCP transports enforce maximum payload size limits.
MCP servers sign tool responses with a unique nonce and timestamp so MCP clients can detect replay attempts.
MCP clients present users with explicit consent dialogue and cancellation options upon installation of a local MCP server.
MCP clients maintain a snapshot of tool definitions and that any change to a tool definition triggers re-approval before the modified tool can be invoked.
MCP proxy servers using a shared upstream OAuth client identity do not allow a requesting MCP client to inherit authorization established for a different MCP client.

MCP clients bind each approved MCP server's granted consent and authorization to the connection endpoint approved for that server, and require user re-approval before any further interaction once that endpoint changes.
MCP clients reject tool definitions containing invalid mirrored-header annotations, excluding the affected tool rather than the entire tool list.
MCP servers reject requests where mirrored request headers do not match the corresponding request body values, after decoding any encoded header values.
MCP implementations apply resource bounds to schema validation, such as a maximum schema depth, a cap on the total number of nested schema elements, or a per-validation time budget.

MCP implementations do not automatically dereference JSON Schema `$ref` values that resolve to network URIs, and that any opt-in external resolution is disabled by default and rejects loopback, link-local, and private network addresses.
MCP implementations reject schemas that fail to validate due to an unresolved external `$ref` rather than treating them as permissive.

MCP clients and intermediaries reuse cached responses marked with a private cache scope only within the authorization context that produced them, and do not cache results of multi round-trip requests.
MCP servers mark cacheable results containing user-specific or authorization-filtered data with a private cache scope.
MCP servers do not use form-mode elicitation to request secrets or payment credentials, and that in URL-mode elicitation the user completing the flow is the same user who initiated it.
MCP servers exclude end-user credentials and personal data from URL-mode elicitation URLs, and do not issue URLs that are pre-authenticated to a protected resource.
MCP clients require explicit user consent and display the full URL before opening any URL-mode elicitation target, and do not pre-fetch the URL or its metadata.
MCP clients open URL-mode elicitation targets so that neither the client nor the model can observe the page contents or the user's input.

requirements.text: model-inferred sensitive attributes are not directly returned in outputs.
inference endpoints enforce per-principal and global rate limits sized to the extraction threat model, and not solely as a generic API throttle.
model outputs are calibrated to reduce overconfident predictions.
training on sensitive datasets employs differentially-private optimization.
membership-inference attack simulations demonstrate that attack accuracy does not exceed random guessing on evaluated data.
query-pattern analysis feeds an extraction-attempt detector.
raw model outputs are not directly exposed beyond the application backend, and that externally visible responses are calibrated to the extraction risk level.
model watermarking or fingerprinting techniques are applied so that unauthorized copies can be identified.
detection of suspected extraction triggers response measures.

inference endpoints constrain sampling and decoding parameters supplied by untrusted callers (e.g., temperature, top-k, top-p, logit bias, candidate/n count) to server-side approved ranges and defaults, rejecting out-of-policy values.
inputs from external or untrusted sources pass through anomaly detection before model inference.
inputs flagged as anomalous trigger gating actions.
the safety violation feedback pipeline includes poisoning detection and human review gates to prevent adversarial manipulation of the improvement mechanism.
AI interactions are logged with session context and AI-specific telemetry.
safety filtering and policy decisions are logged with sufficient detail to support audit, debugging, and forensic analysis of content moderation systems.
log entries for AI inference events follow a structured, interoperable schema that includes at least the model identifier, token usage (input and output), provider name, and operation type.
RAG pipeline retrieval events are logged, including the query, documents retrieved, and knowledge source.
the system detects and alerts on known jailbreak patterns, prompt injection attempts, and adversarial inputs.
behavioral anomaly detection identifies unusual conversation patterns, excessive retry attempts, or probing behaviors.
custom rules detect AI-specific threat patterns for coordinated jailbreak attempts, prompt injection, and system prompt extraction attempts.
extraction-alert events include offending query metadata to support investigation.
token usage is tracked at granular attribution levels including per user, per session, per feature endpoint, and per team or workspace.
LLM API traffic is monitored for covert-channel indicators and communication signatures to identify malware and command-and-control (C2) activity.

data drift detection monitors input distribution changes that may impact model performance, using statistically validated methods matched to the input data type (e.g., KS test or PSI for tabular numeric features, embedding-distance metrics for text or image).

requirements.text: hallucination detection monitors identify and flag model outputs that contain factually incorrect, inconsistent, or fabricated information.

dataset lineage records each dataset and its components, including all transformations, augmentations, and merges.
